correctness.rationale: The complex Pluecker degree is the rectangular hook-length number and the Euler characteristic is the binomial count of Schubert cells. For two-row rectangles, the degree is Catalan; direct boundary values and a strict ratio comparison give exactly the three exceptions. For at least three rows, an explicit injection from 3-by-q tableaux into q-by-q tableaux reduces the square endpoint to a one-variable hook formula, whose ratio dominates the central-binomial ratio from q=3 onward. For fixed q>=3, the degree growth ratio in the other rectangle side strictly exceeds the Euler growth ratio, so the square inequality propagates to every rectangle. All inequalities are strict, proving the absence of equality.

originality.rationale: The primary archival source gives the Grassmannian degree formula and rectangular-tableau interpretation but does not compare it with the topological Euler characteristic. Targeted searches for degree-versus-Euler inequalities, maximal chains versus cells in the Grassmannian Bruhat interval, and rectangular standard-tableau versus rectangle-partition counts did not locate the sharp three-exception classification. The closest indexed results concern log-concavity of Grassmannian degrees or Chow/Hurwitz degree ratios, which are different comparisons and do not imply the stated threshold.
residual_risks: The inequality is elementary once the two classical formulas are juxtaposed, so an older combinatorics source may contain it without Grassmannian terminology.
No claim is made for analogous degree-versus-Euler thresholds on other homogeneous varieties.

value.rationale: The comparison is intrinsic rather than an arbitrary pairing: the Schubert decomposition identifies the Euler characteristic with the number of elements of the same rectangular Bruhat interval whose maximal saturated chains are counted by the Pluecker degree. The theorem gives a complete crossover classification for these two canonical complexity measures, with no equality cases and only three non-projective exceptions. This supplies a clean benchmark for how quickly enumerative complexity overtakes topological cell complexity in the fundamental homogeneous family.
